evidence_works.detail: Acoustic measurements on 1950s archival and 2004-2005 recordings confirm that Washo stressed syllables are kept heavy: long vowels are about twice as long as short ones, and a post-tonic consonant after a short stressed vowel is about 54% longer than after a long one, with ejectives and plain stops geminating too, contrary to Jacobsen's description. Stress is assigned to stems and is generally penultimate, with a small set of final-stress stems whose tonic vowel is always long; the current generation's post-tonic geminates are shorter than the earlier generation's.

3212.dq: Phonological words are mainly monosyllabic or disyllabic. The first syllable of disyllabic words is always unstressed and restricted to three types. ... The major syllable is always stressed and may contain either a long or short monopthong or a dipthong. (sec. 2.1)
3212.prule: Fixed on the main (= word-final) syllable: every word is a monosyllable or a sesquisyllable (unstressed optional presyllable + stressed obligatory main syllable); the presyllable, with vowel a/u/i or a syllabic nasal, is never stressed. Weight plays no role (the presyllable is reduced by definition; the main syllable is stressed whatever its shape).
3212.srule: Not mentioned in the primary source (Miller & Miller 1995, sec.5 pp.45-46) nor in Theraphan 1980 (sec.2, pp.222-223), Tebow 2010 (sec.2.1, p.16) or Tebow & Lew 2013 (sec.3, pp.129-130). For Dong Luang So (Bru), Jungprasert 1986:26-27 (phonology after Darunee Kulachol 1986) states that a full-vowel 'minor syllable' C(C)V(C), the first syllable of a disyllable, 'take[s] secondary stress' before the primary-stressed final major syllable (/ki:ka:jʔ/ 'lazy', /lambʌ: 'convenient', /pruŋpri: 'fruitful'), whereas Ca and syllabic-nasal presyllables are 'always unstressed'.

3213.tone: Eight lexical tones per syllable in Fenghuang Xong (Yankan variety; Shanjiang and Zhuigaolai have an extra sandhi tone -c; Jiwei standard has 6 tones per Sposato p. 95), each a pitch-height + contour + phonation source list, functioning only to distinguish lexical items (/ta2/ 'to precipitate' vs /ta5/ 'to kill' vs /ta7/ 'maternal grandmother'); regular phonologically triggered tone sandhi (secs. 3.5.2.2, 3.5.3); a handful of toneless particles/interjections (sec. 3.6, 9.2.1, 11.3). Superimposed phrase-level intonation: utterance-final fall, emphasis/focus by 'exaggerating' tones (longer level tones, sharper falls), suspected interrogative intonation. A full-text search of the whole grammar: 'stress' occurs only rhetorically ('it must be stressed'), 'prominent' only non-phonologically; no accent/iambic/unstressed/reduced-syllable statements. Family-level remark elsewhere: Ratliff 2010:199 'In form, Hmong-Mien nominal prefixes are open syllables... They are unstressed' -- not Xong-specific; Sposato's Xong prefixes (ghaob- etc.) bear full tone -b and undergo regular sandhi with no reduction remark.

3215.prule: Tone language, no stress rule stated. H vs L is contrastive (ŋ̀ ‘moi’ vs ŋ́ ‘nous’, ì ‘toi’ vs í ‘eux’); H is analysed as the sole underlying (marked) tone with L assigned by default (§3.5); two successive syllables never both carry level H; lexemes fall into two major classes, toneless or with a single H on the first tone-anchoring point (initial syllable), the initial H being 'obligatoirement limité à la syllabe initiale'; a post-lexical demarcative H is inserted on the last toneless TBU of a prosodic word before an L-initial word (§3.7.5). Creissels notes the H/L asymmetry 'évoque... le contraste entre syllabes accentuées et atones dans un système à accent de mot' but says other aspects would be problematic for an accentual analysis and posits no word stress.
3215.srule: Not mentioned in Creissels 2013, ch. 3 'Tonologie' §§3.1-3.7.6, pp. 18-34 (tone-only analysis; no word stress posited, hence no secondary stress)
3215.quote: Il y a en maninka du Niokolo une forte dissymétrie entre ton haut et ton bas. En effet, on peut trouver des séquences de syllabes à ton bas de longueur quelconque, mais on n’a jamais deux syllabes successives à ton ponctuel haut. 3215.idn: maninka du Niokolo (mániŋkakáŋo), spoken by the Mandingues du Niokolo between the town of Kédougou and the Niokolo park, Sénégal Oriental (villages along the Gambia river and in the Haut-Niokolo) (a named variety of the language); data: 'enquêtes réalisées à Kédougou de 2010 à 2012' with consultant Luc Yéra Camara…
3215.tone: Fully tonal description (ch. 3, pp. 18-37): two level tones H/L plus contour realisations analysed as sequences of level tones on one syllable; H the only underlying tone, L by default; non-adjacency of H across syllables; lexical classes = toneless vs initial-H (plus minor classes with a non-initial H); post-lexical demarcative H at prosodic-word boundaries; tonal compactness in nominal compounds. The only place word accent is discussed is §3.4.1 p. 22 (a full-text search for accent/intensité/proéminence/culminatif confirms), where an accentual analysis is evoked and explicitly declined ('d’autres aspects qui poseraient problème pour une analyse accentuelle'). No stress/intensity accent is posited anywhere.

tn.quote: Outre les tons ponctuels haut (H) et bas (B), on peut observer en maninka du Niokolo les modulations suivantes: ton modulé montant BH, modulé descendant HB, doublement modulé BHB, doublement modulé HBH et triplement modulé HBHB. ... On peut donc poser que les tons modulés sont la réalisation de séquences de tons ponctuels (B+H, H+B, B+H+B ou H+B+H+B) associées à une syllabe unique, et qu’en règle générale les syllabes légères comportent un seul point d’ancrage tonal (PAT), alors que les syllabes lourdes en comportent deux.
tn.translation: Besides the level tones high (H) and low (B), one observes in Niokolo Maninka the following modulations: rising BH, falling HB, doubly modulated BHB, doubly modulated HBH and triply modulated HBHB. ... One can therefore posit that the modulated tones are the realisation of sequences of level tones (B+H, H+B, B+H+B or H+B+H+B) associated with a single syllable, and that as a rule light syllables have a single tone-anchoring point (PAT), whereas heavy syllables have two.

3215.cfw: Creissels 2013, the only modern first-hand description of Niokolo Maninka, analyses it as a tone language with two lexical tone classes, a single underlying high tone and a ban on adjacent high tones, and the only dissent is Delafosse 1929, a pan-Manding grammar written before tone was recognised in Manding, which denies tone and puts a weak pitch accent on the last syllable of the word.

3216.heavy: Long syllables consist of a long vowel, or a vowel sequence that functions as a single syllable (the diphthongs ai, au, ei, eu, iu, oi, ou) or of long m̄; a long syllable is approximately equivalent in duration to two short syllables; ea, ia, oa, ua, ie, ue form two short syllables. Short syllables = V or CV (no codas).
3216.dflt: penultimate syllable of the measure (so word-penult for a word of one measure and for the final measure of a longer word)
3216.prule: Stress unit = the measure (at most three syllables, one stress each). Every long syllable (long vowel, diphthong ai/au/ei/eu/iu/oi/ou, or long m̄) is stressed; a measure of short syllables is stressed on its penult; a measure ending in a long syllable is stressed on that final long syllable (tarā, kwadrē, cavā). I.e. within the measure: final if heavy, else penult (right-aligned moraic trochee, the Standard Fijian pattern). A measure cannot be long+short, so a long vowel shortens before a cliticised short syllable (vū+ni kai -> vunikai).
3216.srule: One stress per measure: an orthographic word of two or more measures (measure = one long syllable, two or three short syllables, or short + long syllable, at most three syllables) carries a stress in each measure, placed by the measure rule (kivi+laki+nia, vaka+tunu+loa, vatu+nareba; two adjacent long syllables = two measures, both stressed: rātū, vōvō). The source gives no ranking of these word-internal stresses as primary vs secondary.
3216.quote: A measure is a unit of speech of not more than three syllables, that has one stressed syllable. It may consist of a single long syllable, e.g. kwā, mē, kwai, vou, of two or three short syllables, e.g. ciwa, vatu, alewa, tamata, na vatu, or of a short syllable plus a long syllable, e.g. cavā, rogō, tubā, vecē, na kai. Stress falls on any long syllable and on the penultimate syllable of a measure consisting of short syllables, e.g. ciwa, noa, vatu, tamata, alewa or on the final syllable of a measure that ends in a long syllable, e.g. tarā, kwadrē. 3218.prule: An intonation (pitch) peak falls on the penultimate syllable of the intonation group: the group is defined so that exactly one syllable follows the peak. A word cited alone carries the peak on its penult (bátaq, díyaq, qEbága, qE-dúma, bégas, dúqen); a following monosyllabic enclitic joins the group and moves the peak to the host's final syllable (batáq a, qEbagá ded, qE-dumá qa, qE-genát ka); disyllabic enclitic strings carry it themselves (kÉy-qen, qÉdin, EpÉbes). Clause-length utterances have one peak, optionally two, and in running speech not every content word carries one (geli, mEbegat unpeaked on p. 6). Word-final a reduces to E when it becomes pre-peak. Nothing is said about word stress as such: the word 'stress' never occurs and no stress phoneme is listed in any Elkins inventory (1953, 1967, 1970; Reid 1971 p. 32).

3222.exc_quote: [sec. 6, p. 36] Stress: a large number of Spanish loans follow the Nahuatl stress pattern (see 3.2); thus in transcribing texts the present writer has adopted the practice of marking stress only where it deviates from the usual pattern. Examples: ictoya se λa·kaλ ka ikarabinah the man was there with his carbine (cf. S karabína carbine); mexór ma: kiti·wakan better if they do it (cf. S mexór better). [also p. 36] Other Spanish loans retain their original shape. Examples: N dulses < S dúlses candy; N pastór < S pastór shepherd; ... N mexór < S mexór better.

3222.sec_quote: Words of three or more syllables show in addition secondary stress on the first syllable in phrase initial, and in phrase medial when preceded by a polysyllable. Preceded by a monosyllable, a polysyllable shows only primary stress on the penult; secondary stress falls on the monosyllable, provided it is not one of those bearing primary stress. Other monosyllables are unstressed.

3223.exq_: No stress rule is stated, so no exceptions to one. The exceptions the source names are to its tonal generalisation: 'The phonological word (with a few exceptions) has at least one high tone' (p. 20); 'There is no word larger than one syllable without tones (except kum'e 'or')' (p. 488); postpositio…
3223.tone: Source's own label: 'Laguna is a pitch-accent language' (p. 20) and 'Keresan is a pitch accent language, using only high and low tones; the melody is high/low for most of the dialects, but not for Laguna or Acoma' (pp. 481-482). Five phonetic tones LO, HI, FA (long vowels only), RI (long vowels only), GL (high level + glottal closure), analysed as underlying HI/LO with FA = HILO, RI = LOHI, GL = HI'; a 'positive low' (grave) that blocks devoicing vs a 'residual low' (= absence of HI). Order restrictions (pp. 23-24, 488-489): FA is always the last tone; no long vowel before the first HI; never two contours per word (except two GL); overall melody LO RI HI FA LO. Disyllabic melodies in Table 41 (p. 485) include HIHI, HILO, LOHI, RILO, GLLO, FALO, so HI position is not positional. Tone is 'morphemic' (distinguishes verb themes, e.g. s'aukayutsa pairs, p. 480) and shifts under inflection (siusee'e vs kusee'e, p. 481). Stress is mentioned only in passing: 'the final /a/ in s'idya does have more stress than final the /a/ in, for example shina 'louse'' (p. 481) and 'the possibility of a combination of stress and tone should not be ignored, nor the interaction with intonation' (p. 492); Miller 1965 sec. 137 on Acoma, as reported by Valiquette p. 278, has 'accents consist of pitch, stress, and glottal features', and Strauss & Furch 1982 (ms.) treat Acoma tonal accent, stress and devoicing as foot-based (p. 471). No stress rule anywhere.

3228.prule: No general rule: 'en términos fonológicos... se puede describir el acento prosódico del idioma como libre'; primary stress is contrastive (minimal pairs) and 'no es generalmente predecible'. Within that, the default pattern is word-final primary stress: the general rule for nouns of every class and length (absolute, dependent, compounds) is final primary stress, assigned to the last syllable regardless of syllable weight, and the author's 2017 grammar says 'la gran mayoría de las palabras son agudas'. Quality words are mostly final but include paroxytone/proparoxytone items; verbs are 'mucho más compleja': many one-suffix verbs are paroxytone, with several suffixes stress lands on one of the last two syllables, and suffixes differ in whether they attract stress.
3228.srule: At most two stresses per word: primary on the final syllable and a secondary stress on the syllable containing the word's single long vowel (VV; VC is not heavy) when that syllable is not final; words with no long vowel, or with the long vowel in the final syllable, have only the final stress. Non-rhythmic (no alternating stresses).

3230.prule: Primary stress on the first vowel (= first syllable) of any word; in a compound it may instead fall on the first vowel of the last stem, depending on grammatical structure. quantity-insensitive: vowel quality and length distinctions are confined to stressed nuclei (stress conditions length, not the reverse); non-initial unstressed vowels surface as schwa / syllabic consonants, analysed as unstressed /a/.
3230.srule: Secondary stress falls on the other (non-primary) full vowels of the word, i.e. on non-initial syllables whose nucleus is a chart vowel rather than reduced unstressed /a/ (schwa/syllabic consonant); placement follows vowel quality, not syllable count, and no rhythmic algorithm is given. A non-initial /a/ bearing secondary stress is written with a grave: /ngathàna/ [ŋátàn(a)] vs /puthana/ [pútən(a)]; non-initial compound stems bear secondary stress, signalled by the hyphen (/ma'a-ngamala/).

3231.prule: Primary word stress on the initial syllable: a left-aligned system with a leftmost stress rule (Smith & Johnson 2000 as characterised by Verstraete 2021, who lists Kugu Nganhcara among the Middle Paman languages with 'a reliable description of word stress' of this kind; Blevins 2025, after the same primary, presupposes a 'short initial stressed syllable'). quantity-insensitivity is NOT stated by either carrier; it is inferred: Verstraete's fn.5 raises syllable-weight complications only for Umpila 'due to the occurrence of vowel length beyond the first syllable', Blevins reports stress on a SHORT initial syllable, and Smith & Johnson 1986: 36 say the long/short vowel contrast is 'generally restricted to initial syllables', so no non-initial syllable can be heavy by vowel length and a leftmost rule reduces to fixed initial stress. Phonetic prominence is weak: Smith 1986 calls the Muminh patrilect syllable-timed with initial syllables only about 20% longer.
3231.srule: Not mentioned in Verstraete 2021, sec. 3.3 (author postprint pp.17-18 read in full; the p.18 remark on 'secondary stress on alternate syllables' is generic to Pama-Nyungan and not applied to Kugu Nganhcara), nor in Blevins 2025: 142; the first-hand description (Smith & Johnson 2000, HAL 5: 357-489) has not been opened.

3232.heavy: Three structural grades 'determined by the presence or absence of length and semi-vowels': light = 'short vowels not followed by a semi-vowel'; heavy = 'short vowels followed by a semi-vowel (which may be a member of the next syllable)'; extra heavy = 'long vowels' (pp. 40-41). A coda consonant other than a semi-vowel confers no weight (syllable canon CV, CV·, CVC, CV·C, p. 27). Stress moves to the second syllable only when it is of a strictly higher grade than the first.
3232.dflt: initial: the first syllable following the plus (or hyphen) juncture, also when both syllables are of equal grade (e.g. [kírim] 'cat, obj. case', light-light; [bé·lè·s] 'it could be', extra heavy-extra heavy, p. 43) or the first is heavier ([máyum] 'feet, obj.', heavy-light) and when a heavier syllable is third or later (only secondary stress there)
3232.prule: Within the phonemic word (the stretch bounded by plus juncture /+/, coterminous with informant citation words) there is exactly one prominent syllable of higher pitch and primary stress; it is 'always the first syllable following the juncture unless the second syllable is heavier in which case the second syllable is stressed' (p. 41). Weight is a three-grade scale: light = short vowel not followed by a semi-vowel; heavy = short vowel followed by a semi-vowel; extra heavy = long vowel. Examples p. 41: [cíyel] 'one to be squashed', [ciyí·ya] 'to be all squashed up', [ciyé·da] 'I squashed them up'. A word-internal hyphen juncture /-/ (after a few prefixes, within a few compounds) restarts the computation from the hyphen. Stress is non-phonemic, 'never functional' (p. 27).
3232.srule: Secondary stress is non-rhythmic and weight-driven: every heavy or extra-heavy syllable (short vowel + semivowel, or long vowel) after the primary-stressed syllable carries a secondary stress, proportionately stronger the further it is from the primary; light post-tonic syllables are unstressed (p. 42; table pp. 43-44: S:S: [be:le:s] 'it could be' 1st+2nd, ssS:s [werlebo:sken] 'you will have to come' 1st+3rd, sssS: [kenehale:s] 'it might be' 1st+4th, S:sS: [tu:nuna:] 'to haul big things' 1st+3rd). In words with an internal hyphen juncture /-/ the pre-hyphen part takes only secondary stress, on its first syllable unless its second is heavier (p. 45; [netnen] /+net-nen+/ 'my mother', [wayhola] /+way-hola+/ 'ceremonial pipe', [puba:npurun] /+puba.n-purun+/ 'of those others', p. 46).
